detail.readme:
AX

> [!WARNING] > AX and several of its features are in heavy development. We are actively > refining our core concepts, protocols, and specifications, and will likely > introduce major breaking changes prior to a stable release. **Declare an agentic task with workspaces and model specifications. AX sandboxes it, wires up its workspace, and helps running it at scale.** AX is a highly efficient, declarative orchestrator to run millions of autonomous agent workloads in a cluster. It runs on top of [Agent Substrate](https://github.com/agent-substrate/substrate) for sandboxed execution and is built to run millions of tasks per cluster. If you have used Kubernetes, `ax` will feel similar. ```yaml # task.yaml apiVersion: ax.io/v1alpha1 kind: Workspace metadata: name: golang spec: profile: # tasks that bind this workspace and omit spec.profile use it image: "ghcr.io/my-org/my-coding-agent@sha256:..." setup: git: - repo: https://github.com/golang/go.git ref: "my-fix" files: - path: "AGENTS.md" content: | - Run `go test` to ensure that tests are passing. - Do not modify the public API. --- apiVersion: ax.io/v1alpha1 kind: Task metadata: name: test spec: goal: text: "Fix what's broken please." workspace: name: golang debug: true # enables `ax ssh` ``` Then apply it, resume it, and look over the agent's shoulder: ```bash ax apply -f task.yaml ax resume task test ax describe task test ax ssh test -- ls -al /workspace ``` ## Why? Agents are a new kind of workload. They are neither stateless microservices nor run-to-completion batch jobs. They accumulate state, need strict isolation, call out to model APIs and tool servers, and can burn money in a loop if nobody is watching. AX gives you three small primitives that handle all of that declaratively: | You want to... | AX gives you | |---|---| | Run untrusted agent code in an isolated sandbox with CPU/memory limits | **`Task`** | | Pre-wire Git repos, MCP servers, and skill packages so every agent starts warm | **`Workspace`** | | Configure which LLM the platform itself uses, with credentials from a Kubernetes secret | **`Model`** | | Decide which hosts an agent can reach, and inject credentials without the agent ever seeing them | **`Gateway`** | | Pause an idle agent and pick up exactly where it left off | `ax suspend` / `ax resume` | | Shell into a running agent to see what it is doing | `ax ssh` | Everything is expressed as `ax.io/v1alpha1` manifests and applied with a single command. ## Quick start ### 1. Install the CLI ```bash curl -fsSL https://github.com/google/ax/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh export PATH="$HOME/.ax/bin:$PATH" ``` > [!TIP] > Prefer a UI? [AX Studio](https://github.com/agentexecutor/studio#readme) is a local web app that sets up AX on your computer and starts tasks for you. It deploys its own AX images, so you can skip steps 2 and 3. Install it as its README describes, then run `ax studio`. ### 2. Build the images Until release images are published, build and push your own from an ax checkout and pin them by digest: ```bash export AX_IMAGE_REPO= # e.g. gcr.io/my-project make images # prints the digest of each pushed image export AX_SERVER_IMAGE="$AX_IMAGE_REPO/ax-server@" ``` ### 3. Install AX **Locally**, on a new Kind cluster with Substrate and a WorkerPool: ```bash ax local start --server-image "$AX_SERVER_IMAGE" ``` **On an existing cluster** with Kubernetes 1.37+ and [Agent Substrate](https://github.com/agent-substrate/substrate#readme): ```bash ax install --server-image "$AX_SERVER_IMAGE" ``` Then create a WorkerPool from [`examples/workerpool.yaml`](examples/workerpool.yaml). Without one, tasks fail to resume with `no free workers available`. See the [Local Installer guide](docs/local_installer.md) for prerequisites, `ax uninstall`, and more. ### Run your first task From your ax checkout: ```bash ax apply -f examples/simple.yaml # the smallest useful Task ax resume task simple-task # new tasks start Suspended; resume schedules the actor and starts it ax get tasks # NAME ATESPACE STATE ACTOR AGE # simple-task default Working simple-task 1m ax ssh simple-task -- ls -la /workspace # poke around inside the sandbox ax suspend task simple-task # checkpoint and pause ax resume task simple-task # pick up where it left off ``` The first resume also waits for the workspace to initialize (cloning its git repos), so it can take a while; if the CLI gives up first, the task keeps coming up in the background — `ax get tasks` tells you where it is. Every Task runs an image pinned by digest, named by `spec.profile.image` or `spec.profile.ateTemplate.name` or inherited from its Workspace's `spec.profile`; replace the image in `examples/simple.yaml` with `$AX_TASK_IMAGE` if you built your own. Want to see the whole lifecycle end to end? Run `AX_TASK_IMAGE=... ./demo.sh` ([`demo.sh`](demo.sh)). It applies a custom workspace, resumes the task, runs commands over `ax ssh`, and suspends it again. ## Documentation | Guide | Read it to... | |---|---| | [Local Installer](docs/local_installer.md) | Walk through `ax local`, `ax studio`, `ax ctx`, `ax install`, and promoting tasks unchanged from local Kind to a remote GKE cluster. | | [AX Studio](https://github.com/agentexecutor/studio#readme) | Set up AX on your computer and start, watch, and shell into tasks from a local web app (`ax studio`). | | [Concepts](docs/concepts.md) | Learn what a `Task`, `Workspace`, and `Model` each do, and how a task moves through phases and conditions. | | [Manifests](docs/manifests.md) | Write your own YAML, with an annotated example of every kind. | | [Sandbox](docs/sandbox.md) | See what the runner does on boot and what your command can rely on: metadata server, guest services, environment. | | [Runners](docs/runner.md) | Understand the contract between the control plane and the task container, and build your own runner image to replace the default. | | [Networking](docs/networking.md) | Reach a running task through the atenet router from the cluster, your laptop, or a gRPC client. | | [Observability](docs/observability.md) | Collect ax-server's logs, metrics, traces, and events, and configure where they go. | | [Architecture](DESIGN.md) | Understand how the control plane fits together, plus the [API reference](DESIGN.md#api-reference). | | [Development](docs/development.md) | Build, test, and ship changes to AX itself. | | [Roadmap](docs/roadmap.md) | See planned milestones across core specs, actor architecture, agentic environments, and governance. | ## CLI usage `ax` talks to the control plane over gRPC. It is deliberately `kubectl`-shaped: `apply`, `get`, `describe`, `delete`, plus a few agent-specific verbs. ### Everyday commands ```bash # Apply anything (multi-document YAML, file or stdin) ax apply -f examples/simple.yaml # Tasks ax get tasks # list ax get tasks -a my-atespace # list in another atespace ax get task task123 # full spec + live status as YAML ax describe task task123 # human-readable detail ax suspend task task123 # checkpoint actor state and pause ax resume task task123 # resume a suspended task ax promote task task123 --to prod # copy the task and what it binds to the cluster of kube context prod, and resume it there ax delete task task123 # Shell into the running sandbox ax ssh task123 # interactive shell (task needs spec.debug: true) ax ssh task123 -- ls -la /workspace # one-off command ax ssh task123 -- python3 main.py # Workspaces, gateways, and models follow the same pattern ax get workspaces # NAME ATESPACE GIT-REPOS MCP-SERVERS # default-workspace default 1 1 ax describe workspace default-workspace ax delete workspace default-workspace ax get gateways # NAME ATESPACE EGRESS-RULES # review-bot-gw default 3 ax describe gateway review-bot-gw ax delete gateway review-bot-gw ax get models # NAME ATESPACE PROVIDER MODEL # default-model default google gemini-3.8-flash ax describe model default-model ax delete model default-model # Environment & connection plumbing ax local start --server-image # create/resume local Kind + Substrate + AX cluster ax local status # check local environment, Substrate, and AX health ax local stop # stop local environment while keeping state ax local delete # destroy local environment and clean up owned context ax install / ax uninstall # install or remove AX on the active Kubernetes cluster ax studio # launch the AX Studio local Web UI on 127.0.0.1:8080 (needs the ax-studio binary) ax ctx # list kube contexts and active AX tunnel status ax ctx # switch active Kubernetes context in kubeconfig ax tunnel list # background tunnels (state lives in ~/.ax/tunnels) ax tunnel stop ax version ``` ### Works with `kubectx` `ax` follows your active Kubernetes context. Switch clusters and `ax` resolves and tunnels to that cluster's control plane in the background. ```bash kubectx staging-cluster ax get tasks kubectx prod-cluster ax get tasks # Or target a context without switching ax --context=dev-cluster get tasks ``` ### Global flags | Flag | Description | Default | |---|---|---| | `-a`, `--atespace` | Atespace scope for the command | `default` | | `-n`, `--namespace` | Kubernetes namespace where AX is installed | `ax-system` | | `--context` | Kubernetes context to target | active `kubectx` / `current-context` | | `--server` | Control plane address, bypassing auto-detection | derived from kube context, or `$AX_SERVER` | | `--trace` | Trace the command and print its trace ID to stderr. Its RPCs send a sampled W3C `traceparent`, and CLI spans are exported over OTLP when `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT` is set. Without it, the CLI sends no trace context and ax-server samples on its own. See [CLI traces](docs/observability.md#cli-traces) | off | ## License Apache License 2.0. See [LICENSE](LICENSE) for details.
